passages.title: Twelve Cookies
sentences: Grandma Rose gave Sam twelve cookies.
"Share them with your friends," she said.
Sam sat on the steps with Priya, Leo and Maya.
He gave each friend three cookies.
He kept three for himself.
Leo counted his cookies.
Then he counted Sam's.
"We all have the same," Leo said. "That is fair."

passages.title: Turns on the Big Ramp
sentences: On Sunday, the big ramp at the skate park was busy.
Some older kids took turn after turn.
A small boy named Jai stood by the side with his board.
He waited and waited.
Leo saw him and had an idea.
He took a marker and a piece of cardboard out of his bag.
"Let's make a list," he said. "Each person gets one turn, then goes to the back."
He wrote every name on the list, and Jai's name went on too.
The older kids grumbled at first.
Then they saw that everyone got lots of turns.
When Jai rolled down the ramp, the whole line cheered.

passages.title: The Fox and the Stork
sentences: One day, a fox asked a stork to come for dinner.
The fox served soup in a wide, flat dish.
He lapped up his soup fast.
The stork had a long, thin beak.
Her beak tapped the flat dish, but she got only a few drops.
The fox grinned at her.
The next week, the stork asked the fox to dinner.
She served soup in a tall jar with a narrow neck.
The stork dipped her long beak in and drank it all.
The fox could only lick the outside of the jar.
He went home hungry.
"Now you know how it feels," said the stork.

credit.title: The Fox and the Stork
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Honest Woodcutter
sentences: A poor woodcutter was chopping a tree beside a deep river.
His axe slipped out of his hands and fell into the water with a splash.
It was his only axe, and he needed it for his work.
He sat on the bank and put his head in his hands.
Then a river spirit rose up out of the water.
She held up an axe made of shining gold.
"Is this your axe?" she asked.
"That axe is gold," said the woodcutter. "My axe is plain iron."
Next, the spirit held up a silver axe.
"My axe is plain iron," he said again.
At last, she held up his old iron axe.
"Yes, that one is mine!" he said, and he smiled.
The spirit was pleased that he told the truth.
She gave him all three axes to take home.

credit.title: Mercury and the Woodman
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Broken Mug
sentences: After school, Leo and Sam stopped at the Lighthouse Café for hot chocolate.
Leo had his skateboard under his arm.
As he turned to sit down, the end of the board hit a mug on the shelf.
The mug fell to the floor and broke into three pieces.
The café was busy, and the owner, Mrs. Lin, was in the back.
Leo's face went red.
He picked up the pieces and walked to the counter.
"Mrs. Lin, I broke one of your mugs with my board," he said. "I am sorry."
He took four dollars from his pocket.
"I can pay for it," he said.
Mrs. Lin looked at the pieces and then at Leo.
"Thank you for telling me," she said. "That was honest."
"Keep your money. Next time, carry your board by the wheels."

passages.title: The Rematch
sentences: On Friday night, the library held a game night with a racing tournament on the big screen.
Leo and Sam both reached the final race.
The winner would get to choose the first game at the next game night.
Halfway around the track, Sam's car was in the lead.
Then a boy hurried past and caught his foot on Sam's controller cord.
The cord pulled out of the console, and Sam's car rolled to a stop.
Leo's car raced past and crossed the finish line first.
"Leo wins!" announced the librarian.
Leo did not cheer.
"That win does not count," he said. "Sam's controller came unplugged in the middle of the race."
"Can we race again?"
The librarian plugged the cord back in and started a new race.
This time, Leo won by exactly one second.
Sam shook his hand and smiled.
"Now that is a real win," Sam said.

passages.title: The Oxen and the Wheels
sentences: Two strong oxen were pulling a heavy wagon along a muddy country road.
The wagon was loaded with sacks of grain for the market in town.
The mud was deep, so the oxen had to pull with all their strength.
Step by step, they dragged the heavy wagon forward.
They did not make a sound.
The wagon's wheels had a much easier job, because all they had to do was turn.
But with every turn, they creaked and groaned loudly.
"Oh, this terrible road!" the wheels cried. "We are working so hard!"
At last, the oxen stopped and looked back at the noisy wheels.
"Why are you making so much noise?" asked one ox.
"We are the ones doing the heavy work, and we are not complaining at all."

credit.title: The Oxen and the Wheels
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Tooth in the Sand
sentences: Ms. Ortiz's class spent a Friday morning at a fossil dig in the hills above Story Woods.
A guide from the town museum gave each pair of students a small square of ground, a soft brush and a trowel.
"Scientists have found dinosaur bones on this hill before," she said.
"Everything you find today belongs to the museum, so please call me before you lift anything out."
Maya and Sam brushed the sandy soil away slowly, one thin layer at a time.
After an hour, Sam went to refill their water bottles, and Maya kept working alone.
Then her brush uncovered something dark and pointed, about as long as her thumb.
Along one edge was a row of tiny bumps.
Maya had a box of rocks and crystals at home, but she had never found a fossil.
Nobody was looking, and the dark thing would fit easily in her pocket.
Maya looked at it for a long time.
Then she stood up and waved to the guide.
The guide knelt beside the square and let out a gasp.
"This is a tooth from a meat-eating dinosaur," she said. "The tiny bumps helped it cut its food."
She wrote down exactly where the tooth lay and which layer of rock it came from, because that helps scientists learn how old a fossil is.
A month later, the class visited the museum.
The tooth sat in a glass case, and the card beside it said, "Found by Maya Brooks, Harbor Middle School."
Maya still wished she could hold it in her hand.
But she stood by the case for a long time and read the card three times.

passages.title: Three Names on the Card
sentences: For six weeks, Priya, Ben and Leo designed and built a robot for the Harbor Middle School robot fair.
The robot had to follow a black line across the gym floor and stop exactly on a red square.
Priya built the body, connected the motors and wrote almost all of the computer code.
Leo painted the robot bright blue and named it Comet.
Ben missed many meetings because of soccer practice, but he tested Comet twice on the practice track.
On the day of the fair, Comet followed the line without a single mistake and stopped right on the red square.
The judges awarded the team a blue ribbon.
The robot club had a rule that the whole team shares every prize, so the ribbon card listed all three names.
When a judge asked who had written the code, Ben and Leo both turned to look at Priya.
Later, Priya spoke quietly to Ms. Ortiz, who runs the robot club.
"I am glad we won," she said. "But I did most of the work, and the card makes it look like we all did the same amount."
Ben was packing up the table nearby, and he heard every word.
He thought about it all through lunch, and afterward he made a new sign for the team's table.
It said, "Body, motors and code: Priya. Paint and name: Leo. Testing: Ben."
"The ribbon belongs to the whole team," Ben explained to Priya. "But visitors should know who actually built Comet."
Priya read the sign carefully, and then she smiled.

passages.title: Behind the Screen
sentences: When an orchestra needs a new player, it holds an audition, a short test in which each musician plays alone for a group of judges.
For many years, the judges sat in the same room and watched each player walk in, sit down and play.
They could see each person's face, clothes and age, and they often knew who the player's teacher was.
Some musicians began to wonder whether the judges were choosing the best playing or the people they already liked.
To make the test fairer, many orchestras began to hold blind auditions.
In a blind audition, the musician plays behind a tall screen, so the judges can hear the music but cannot see who is playing.
Each player is called by a number instead of a name.
Some orchestras even lay a carpet on the floor, because the sound of a player's footsteps could give the judges a clue about who was walking in.
In the years after screens came into use, orchestras hired many more women than they had before.
Not everyone agrees that the screen should stay up for the whole audition.
Some judges say that an orchestra player must work closely with other people, and a screen cannot show how well someone listens and follows.
For this reason, many orchestras use the screen in the early rounds and take it away for the final round.
Other people say the screen should stay up until the very end, so that nothing except the music can count.
Both groups want the same thing: a fair test that chooses the best player.
They disagree about how to make the test fair in the last round.
Some school bands now use a screen for solo tryouts too, so every student knows that only the sound will be judged.

passages.title: No Photo, No Score
sentences: Every June, young people fish from the Harbor Town pier in a catch-and-release contest.
When someone catches a fish, they lay it on a measuring board, take a photograph and then gently return it to the sea.
The most important rule is printed on every entry card: "No photo, no score."
The prize for the longest fish is a brand-new fishing rod, donated by the Lighthouse Café.
Near the end of the morning, Leo felt a powerful tug on his line.
He reeled in a silver fish that was longer than his arm, far larger than any other fish caught that day.
Leo wet his hands first, because dry hands can damage the slippery coating that protects a fish's skin, and then he lifted it toward the board.
At that moment, the fish gave a strong flip, slid out of his hands and splashed back into the water.
Ana had been fishing beside him, and she had witnessed the whole thing.
Leo and Ana walked to the judges' table, where Mr. Okafor was recording the scores.
Leo explained exactly what had happened, and Ana added that she had seen the fish too.
Mr. Okafor listened carefully, and then he slowly shook his head.
"I believe you both," he said. "But if I give a score for a fish that was never measured, I would have to do the same for every person here."
"Then the measuring board and the photographs would not mean anything."
Ana frowned. "That does not seem fair to Leo," she said.
Leo was quiet for a moment, and then he answered, "It is the same rule for everyone."
The prize went to Ben, whose fish was about half as long as Leo's.
Ben held up his new rod, and then he walked over and invited Leo to share it with him for the rest of the summer.
On the walk home, Leo admitted that he still wished he had taken that photograph.
However, he also said he was glad the contest had been fair to everyone.

passages.title: The Dog in the Manger
sentences: A dog lay down for a nap in a manger, a long wooden box that holds hay for cows.
The manger stood in a warm, quiet barn on a farm.
Late in the afternoon, the cows came in from the field, tired and very hungry.
They walked over to the manger to eat their hay.
The dog jumped up and barked at them.
"Go away!" he growled. "This is my bed."
The cows stepped back in surprise.
"You do not even eat hay," said one cow. "Why keep it from us?"
The dog only barked louder.
Then the farmer came in and saw everything.
He sent the dog out of the barn, and the hungry cows finally ate their dinner.

credit.title: The Dog in the Manger
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Plane Tree
sentences: Two travelers walked along a dusty road on a hot summer day.
There was no wind, and the sun was very strong.
At noon, they came to a plane tree, a tall tree with wide green leaves.
They lay down in its cool shade to rest.
One traveler looked up at the branches.
"This tree is no use to anyone," he said.
"It has no fruit, and it drops leaves all over the road."
Then a voice came from the branches.
"You are lying in my shade right now," said the tree.
"I am keeping you cool on a hot day, and you still say I am no use!"
The travelers looked at each other and said nothing.

credit.title: The Plane Tree
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Travelers and the Purse
sentences: Two travelers were walking together along a dusty country road.
One of them spotted a leather purse lying in the dirt, and he picked it up.
It was heavy with coins.
"Look what I have found!" he said happily.
"Do not say 'I have found,'" said his friend. "We are traveling together, so say 'we have found.'"
"No," said the first traveler. "I saw it first, so it belongs to me."
A few minutes later, they heard loud voices behind them.
A group of people was hurrying down the road, looking at the ground.
"We have lost our purse!" they called. "Has anyone seen it?"
The first traveler began to worry that the people would think he had stolen it.
"We are in trouble now," he whispered to his friend.
His friend shook his head.
"When you found the purse, you said 'I,'" he answered.
"So now you must say, 'I am in trouble.'"
The first traveler walked back alone and handed the purse to its owners.

credit.title: The Travelers and the Purse
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Monkey and the Cat
sentences: A monkey and a cat lived in the same house.
One cold evening, a pan of chestnuts was roasting in the hot coals of the fireplace.
The nuts smelled wonderful, and the monkey wanted every one of them.
"Cat, you have such quick paws," said the monkey. "You are much better at this than I am."
"Pull the chestnuts out of the fire, and we will share them."
The cat felt proud of the praise.
She reached in carefully and pulled out one chestnut.
The coals were hot, and the tips of her paws stung.
While she reached in again, the monkey cracked the first nut and ate it.
The cat pulled out nut after nut, and the monkey ate each one.
Then their owner came into the room, and both animals ran away.
The cat had sore paws and not a single chestnut.
After that, she stayed away from the monkey and his nice words.

credit.title: The Monkey and the Cat
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Window Seat
sentences: On Saturday morning, Sam and Ben rode the train to a model train show in the city.
Sam had ridden this line many times, but it was Ben's first trip.
Their two seats had only one window between them.
Sam loved to watch the tracks curve along the coast, and he wanted the window seat very much.
He also knew that the best views came in the first half of the trip, when the train ran beside the sea.
Ben looked at the window, but he did not say anything.
Sam opened his map of the rail line and counted the stops.
"There are eight stops," he said. "You take the window for the first four, and I will take it for the last four."
Ben grinned and slid into the window seat.
For four stops, he watched waves splash against the rocks below the tracks.
At the fourth stop, Ben stood up without being asked.
"Your turn," he said. "Thanks for giving me the sea part."
Sam watched the bridges and tunnels for the rest of the ride.

passages.title: The Rain Gauge
sentences: Ms. Ortiz's class kept a rain gauge on a post behind Harbor Middle School.
A rain gauge is a clear tube with lines that show how much rain has fallen.
Each day, two students read the tube, wrote the number on a chart and emptied it.
This week, the job belonged to Maya and Ana.
On Wednesday, the girls got busy painting a poster, and they both forgot.
On Thursday morning, the tube held two days of rain mixed together.
"We could split the number in half," said Ana. "Nobody would know."
Maya looked at the chart, which the class would make into a graph.
"But we do not know how much fell on each day," she said.
"If we guess, the graph will look true, but it will not be true."
Ana thought for a moment, and then she nodded.
They wrote the total in Thursday's box with a note: "Two days of rain. We forgot on Wednesday."
Ms. Ortiz thanked them for being honest.
"Scientists make mistakes too," she said. "Good scientists write them down."

passages.title: The Wrong Note
sentences: Ms. Gray's band was practicing a new song for the spring concert.
In the middle of the song, the four flutes played a short part by themselves.
Every time they reached it, one high note sounded wrong.
Ms. Gray stopped the band and listened to the flutes alone.
"One flute is playing an F instead of an F sharp," she said. "Who is it?"
Nobody answered, and the music room became completely silent.
Maya's cheeks felt hot.
She had been playing a plain F, because she had missed the sharp sign in her music.
Maya felt uncomfortable speaking in front of the whole band.
But she knew the other flute players might get the blame, and the song would keep sounding wrong.
She raised her hand. "It was me," she said quietly.
Ms. Gray nodded and smiled. "Thank you, Maya. That took courage."
She pointed to the small sharp sign printed next to the note, and the band practiced the part again.
This time, all four flutes sounded exactly right together.

passages.title: The Honey in the Hollow Tree
sentences: High in a hollow oak tree, someone had built a large honeycomb packed with golden honey.
One morning, a group of bees and a group of wasps both arrived at the tree, and each group claimed that the honey belonged to them.
The argument grew so loud that every creature in the forest could hear it.
At last, the two sides agreed to let an old hornet act as judge, since he had settled many arguments before.
The hornet began by calling witnesses to describe what they had seen.
An ant reported that she had noticed striped, winged insects buzzing around the tree for weeks.
Unfortunately, bees and wasps are both striped, winged insects that buzz, so her report did not settle anything.
Every other witness said much the same thing, and the hornet could not decide.
He announced that the case would continue in six weeks.
Then a wise old bee asked to speak.
"Six weeks is far too long," she said. "By then, the honey may spoil."
"Here is a fair test: let each side build a new honeycomb and fill it with honey."
"Then the judge can see which side is able to make honey like this."
The wasps quickly complained that the test was unfair, and they refused to take part.
The hornet turned to the crowd and gave his decision.
"The wasps will not take the test, so it is clear who made this honeycomb," he said. "The honey belongs to the bees."

credit.title: The Bees and Wasps, and the Hornet
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Half of Every Game
sentences: Coach Novak's soccer team had one rule that never changed: every player plays at least half of every game.
The team had fifteen players but only eleven places on the field, so some players always had to wait on the bench.
Coach Novak kept a clipboard with every name on it and wrote down how many minutes each person played.
In the league final, the score was tied at halftime.
Ana had played the whole first half, and she had scored the team's only goal.
Four players had not played at all yet, including a girl who had joined the team in the spring and had never scored.
Coach Novak checked the clipboard and called Ana over to the bench.
A few parents groaned, and Ben whispered, "We need Ana on the field if we want to win."
At first, Ana felt frustrated as she sat down on the bench.
Then she remembered her own first season, when she was the newest player and the rule had given her a chance to play in big games.
She cheered loudly for the girl from the spring, who ran hard and blocked two shots.
Near the end, the other team scored, and that team won the final by one goal.
On the walk home, Ben said the rule had cost them the trophy.
Ana answered that it might have, but the same rule had also helped her become the player she was now.
"A team is everyone on it," she said, "not just the eleven people on the field at the end."

passages.title: Rules of the Gold Camps
sentences: In 1848, people found gold in a river in California, and soon thousands of people rushed there hoping to get rich.
At first, there were almost no laws or police in the gold fields.
So in many mining camps, the miners met together and voted on their own rules.
Most camps had rules about claims.
A claim was a small piece of ground along a river where one miner had the right to dig.
To keep things fair, many camps limited how big a claim could be, so that one person could not take a whole riverbank.
A miner usually marked a claim by leaving a wooden stake or a tool in the ground.
If the miner stopped working on the claim for too many days, someone else could take it.
Arguments were often settled at a meeting where the miners listened to both sides and then voted.
These rules were fairer than having no rules at all, but they were not fair to everyone.
Some camps tried to push out miners who had come from other countries, and a state law made many of them pay an extra tax.
The miners at the meeting made the rules, so people who were kept out of the meeting were often treated unfairly.

passages.title: One Look Each
sentences: On a clear night in October, the observatory on Lantern Peaks opened its giant telescope to the public.
The Moon was half full, which is a good time to see craters, because long shadows make every bump easy to see.
More than forty people stood in a line that wound down the observatory's stone steps.
Dr. Lee set a timer beside the eyepiece, the small lens that you look into.
"Everyone gets one minute," she said. "When the timer beeps, please let the next person look."
Leo was near the front of the line, and he planned to photograph the craters by holding his phone up to the eyepiece.
Lining up the phone was much harder than he expected, and every picture came out blurry or bright white.
The timer beeped just as he finally got the craters in the middle of his screen.
"Could I have one more minute, please?" he asked. "I almost have it."
Behind him, a father was holding a small boy who kept yawning and rubbing his eyes.
Dr. Lee explained that the timer let everyone have a first turn before the observatory closed.
"But anyone who wants a second look may join the back of the line," she added.
Leo looked at the sleepy boy, put his phone away and walked down to the end of the line.
Forty minutes later, he reached the telescope again, and this time he knew exactly how to hold the phone.
His photo showed rows of sharp gray craters, and that night he made it the background on his phone.
He told his friends that waiting had been boring, but it felt better than taking a turn from someone who had not looked yet.

passages.title: The Printer Sign-Up Sheet
sentences: The robot club at Harbor Middle School had one 3D printer, and almost every member wanted to use it.
A 3D printer builds a solid object one thin layer of plastic at a time, so even a small part can take hours to finish.
To keep things fair, Ms. Ortiz made a sign-up sheet with two-hour slots, and each member could sign up for only one slot each week.
On Tuesday, the back wheel of Priya's rover cracked during a test run.
The rover race was on Saturday, and printing a new wheel would take almost two hours.
Priya's slot was not until the following Monday, and every slot before Saturday was already full.
Ben had signed up for the Thursday slot.
Priya asked Ms. Ortiz whether she could have an extra slot, just this once.
"I can't move other people's names for you," Ms. Ortiz said. "That would not be fair to them."
"But members are allowed to trade slots if both people agree."
Ben was planning to print a stand for his game controller, which he did not need by any special day.
Still, he had been waiting all week, and he had already finished the design.
Priya explained the problem and offered him her Monday slot in exchange.
Ben thought about it, and then he crossed out his name on the Thursday line and wrote hers.
"My controller stand can wait until Monday," he said. "Your race can't."
On Saturday, the rover crossed the finish line on its new wheel, and Ben was the first person Priya thanked.

passages.title: The Pizza Problem
sentences: On Friday evening, Priya, Leo, Ben and Maya met at Priya's house to finish a science project.
By six o'clock everyone was hungry, so they ordered one large pizza that cost twelve dollars and came cut into twelve slices.
Leo, Ben and Maya each had only two dollars with them.
Priya had more money, so she paid the other six dollars.
When the pizza arrived, Ben began to hand out the slices.
"Three slices each," he said. "Twelve slices and four people makes three each, so that is fair."
"Wait," said Leo. "Priya paid half of the money, so maybe she should get half of the pizza."
He counted on his fingers: one slice for each dollar would mean six slices for Priya and two for everyone else.
Ben argued that friends should share equally, no matter who happened to have more money that day.
Leo argued that it was not fair for Priya to pay three times as much and get the same amount.
Maya, who had been quiet, said that she only wanted two slices anyway.
Everyone turned to Priya, because the extra money had been hers.
Priya said she had paid more only because she had more money with her, not because she wanted more pizza.
"Let's split it equally," she said. "Next time, someone else can pay the extra."
They each took three slices, and Maya gave her third slice to Leo, who said it was the best math problem he had ever solved.
Then Ben wrote "Next pizza: Ben pays extra" on a sticky note and stuck it to the empty box.

passages.title: The Donkey's Shadow
sentences: Long ago, a traveler needed to cross a wide, sandy plain to reach a distant town.
The journey would take the whole day, so he rented a donkey from a man who earned his living by hiring out his animals.
The owner walked beside the donkey to guide it, while the traveler rode comfortably on its back.
By noon, the summer sun was scorching, and there was not a single tree anywhere on the plain to offer shade.
The traveler climbed down to rest, and he noticed that the donkey's body cast a dark patch of shade on the sand.
It was the only shade for miles, and it was just large enough for one person.
He sat down in it gratefully, but the owner was exhausted from walking and wanted the shade too.
"Move over," the owner said. "You rented my donkey, but you did not rent its shadow."
"The shadow comes with the donkey," the traveler replied. "I paid for the whole animal for the whole day."
The owner argued that he had agreed to carry a passenger, not to give away the only shade on the plain.
The traveler argued that a rider who pays for a donkey should be able to use every part of it.
Each man was certain that his own reasoning was correct, and their voices grew louder and louder.
Meanwhile, the donkey grew nervous at all the shouting.
It shook its head, turned around and trotted off across the plain toward home.
The two men stopped arguing and stared after it in silence.
Now neither of them had any shade at all, and the traveler had no way to reach the town.
They had argued so hard about the shadow that they had lost the donkey itself.

credit.title: The Ass and His Shadow
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Sharing the Sea
sentences: The ocean can seem endless, but the number of fish in it is not.
If people catch fish faster than the fish can produce young, the number of fish shrinks year after year.
For this reason, many countries set rules about how many fish may be caught, and where and when people may fish.
One common rule is a catch limit, which sets the total weight of one kind of fish that boats may bring in during a year.
Another is a size limit: a fish shorter than a certain length must be put back, so it can grow up and have young of its own.
Some areas also close for part of the year, often during the season when fish gather to lay their eggs.
Scientists count and measure fish every year to help decide what the limits should be.
These rules can be hard on the people who fish for a living.
When a limit is lowered, a crew may earn less money, even though the boat, the fuel and the nets cost just as much as before.
Some fishers say the limits are set too low, or that the scientists' counts are not always correct.
Many fishing families have worked on the water for generations, and they want to help make the rules that affect their work.
People who support the limits point to what can happen without them.
In the early 1990s, a huge cod fishery in the North Atlantic Ocean was closed after the fish became too scarce to catch.
Thousands of people lost their jobs, and many years later the cod had still not returned to their old numbers.
Supporters say a limit that feels unfair today protects the fish, and the jobs, for children who are not old enough to fish yet.
Most people agree that the sea should be shared fairly.
The hard question is how to be fair to the people who fish today and the people who will fish tomorrow at the same time.

passages.title: Making Sport Fair
sentences: In most sports, the fun depends on a fair contest, where nobody wins just because of luck or a better place to stand.
That sounds simple, but wind, sunshine and even the shape of a track can give one player an advantage.
Over many years, people have invented clever rules to make contests more equal.
In soccer, a coin toss helps decide which team starts at which end of the field, and the teams switch ends at halftime.
If a strong wind blows down the field or the sun shines in one goalkeeper's eyes, each team spends half the game facing it.
Tennis players change ends many times during a match for the same reason.
On a running track, the outside lanes curve around a wider circle than the inside lanes.
If every runner in a 400-meter race started on the same line, the runners in the outside lanes would have to run farther.
So the starts are staggered: each lane starts a bit ahead of the one inside it, and every runner covers exactly 400 meters.
Wind matters on the track too: in short sprints, a record does not count if a strong wind was pushing the runners from behind.
Not every rule makes everyone equal, though.
In swimming and running finals, the athletes with the fastest times from the earlier races are given the middle lanes.
Supporters say this rewards the fastest athletes and lets them see their rivals on both sides.
Others say the outer lanes can be harder, because waves in a pool bounce off the side walls, so slower athletes start with an extra problem.
Both sides want a fair race, but they disagree about whether fair means "the same for everyone" or "a reward for doing well."

passages.title: Who Owns a Dinosaur?
sentences: In recent years, a few dinosaur skeletons have been sold at auction for tens of millions of dollars.
At an auction, buyers bid against each other, and the item goes to whoever offers the most money.
Some went to museums, but others went to private buyers, and that worries many scientists.
Who is allowed to sell a fossil depends on where it was found.
In some countries, every dinosaur fossil belongs to the whole country, and selling one is against the law.
In others, such as the United States, a fossil found on private land belongs to the landowner, who may sell it.
But dinosaur bones found on public land there usually must go to a museum or a college.
Scientists who want fossils kept in museums say that science depends on checking each other's work.
If a skeleton sits in a private home, other scientists may never get to measure it again, so no one can check what was learned from it.
For this reason, many scientists will not publish a study about a fossil unless it is kept in a public museum.
They also worry that museums cannot afford such high prices.
People on the other side make their own arguments.
Collectors say that wind and rain slowly wear away bones left in the ground, and that digging them up saves them.
Landowners say that a fossil on their land is theirs, just like the soil or the trees.
Some buyers have also lent or given their skeletons to museums, where anyone can see them.
In the end, this is a hard question about fairness.
Should something that teaches us about the history of life belong to everyone, or to the person who found it or paid for it?

passages.title: Maps for Every Rider
sentences: A transit map is supposed to help every rider get where they are going.
For a long time, though, many maps were made for riders who could see every color, climb any stairs and read small print.
Riders who could not do those things often had to ask for help or guess, and some stayed home rather than risk getting stuck.
Today, many transit maps mark step-free stations, where a person can get from the street to the train without any stairs.
For someone who uses a wheelchair or pushes a stroller, that small symbol can decide whether a trip is possible at all.
Some stations also have tactile maps, with raised lines and braille labels, so people who are blind can read them by touch.
Map makers have also learned that about one in twelve men has trouble telling certain colors apart, especially red and green.
A map that shows two lines only in red and green can be confusing, so careful designers add letters, numbers or patterns to each line.
These changes raise questions without easy answers.
Every new symbol takes up space, and a crowded map can become harder for everyone to read.
Some designers prefer to make one map that works for all riders, even if it has to be plainer.
Others make several maps, each for a different need, but then a rider has to find the right one.
Both groups agree on the goal: a map is only fair if every rider can use it.

passages.title: The Canyon Glitch
sentences: Ben had been practicing the desert track in his favorite racing game for three weeks.
Each track had a leaderboard listing the fastest laps in the world, and Ben's best time was in 512th place.
One evening, he steered too wide on the last corner, hit a rock at a strange angle and landed on the far side of a canyon wall.
His car had skipped almost a quarter of the track, and his lap time was eleven seconds faster than any time on the whole list.
"That's a glitch," said Ana, who was watching from the couch. "It's a mistake in the game's code."
Ben grinned, because a glitch like that could put him at the top of the list by morning.
Ana said that some players hunt for glitches for months, and some games keep separate lists for glitch runs, so finding one takes real skill.
Ben stopped grinning, because he was thinking about the players who drove every corner of the track.
"They practiced for months to get half a second faster," he said. "My lap would move them all down the list, and I skipped the hard part."
Ana argued that the rules page said nothing about glitches, so using one was not cheating.
Ben argued that a rule does not have to be written down for something to be unfair.
Both of them had a point, and they argued about it until dinner.
Afterward, they read the game's help page together and found a form for reporting glitches to the people who made the game.
Ben sent a report that described exactly where the rock was and how he had hit it.
He did not upload his glitch lap to the leaderboard.
Two weeks later, a game update fixed the canyon wall, and the notes for the update thanked "a player who reported the canyon glitch."
Ben's best time was still in 512th place, but he said he would rather move up the list one honest half-second at a time.
